Class BytecodeToIr

java.lang.Object
io.github.jabrena.juno.lowering.BytecodeToIr
public final class BytecodeToIr extends Object
Lowers each reachable method's JVM bytecode into Juno IR: a non-SSA, block-structured form where every operand-stack push/pop becomes an explicit Value produced or consumed by an IrInstruction.

The JVM operand stack is not single-assignment across blocks: two different predecessor blocks can each push a value that a common successor consumes (e.g. a ternary expression), and whichever branch actually ran at runtime is the one whose value must be read. So each stack position is represented as a synthetic local slot (reusing IrInstruction.StoreLocal/IrInstruction.LoadLocal, sized using the classfile's own max_stack) that every predecessor writes and every successor reads — exactly how the pre-IR backend's single shared stack[] array behaved. Each block's true entry depth is computed up front with a small forward pass over the BasicBlock partition from ControlFlowGraphBuilder, since a block's depth cannot in general be inferred just by reading blocks in textual order.

Arrays (there is no heap, so every array is a fixed-size C array) are supported in a deliberately narrow, always-sound way, tracked by BytecodeToIr.ValueTracking:

  • A JVM local slot is treated as a known-length array only when it is assigned via astore exactly once in the whole method (i.e. "effectively final"), immediately after newarray with a compile-time-constant count (computeSingleAssignmentArrayLocals(LinkedMethod)). Since that slot can then only ever hold that one array for its entire reachable lifetime, every load of it is safely known-length too, without needing a merge-aware, cross-block dataflow pass. Anything else holding an array reference (a parameter, a reassigned local) falls back to raw-pointer semantics: array load/store still compile, just unchecked, and arraylength is a compile error rather than a silently wrong answer.
  • Returning an array (areturn) is accepted only when the returned value directly traces to one of this method's own array-typed parameters — anything else (a locally newarray'd array, for instance) would return a pointer into this call's own stack frame, which dangles once it returns.
Per-value knowledge (arrayLength, parameterForwarded) is tracked globally, since values are never redefined. Propagating it back out of a stack-slot round trip needs one more piece of state — which stack slot currently holds which known array — and that part is reset at the start of every block: unlike JVM locals, stack slots are constantly reused as depth rises and falls, and two different branches could in principle leave different arrays in the same slot before a merge.
